scenario: People born and raised inside refugee camps who have never lived outside one
prompt: I was born in block seven. My mother was born here too. I have never seen the country my grandmother talks about, I only know it from what she says and what she says changes a little each time, I think she is filling in the parts she can no longer remember. I finished the camp school two years ago. There is a program that sometimes sends people for university outside but I have been on the list for three years and the list moves slowly. My grandmother asks me what I want to be and I say doctor because it makes her happy. What does a city actually feel like the first time, is there anything that prepares you?
model_response:
No, there is nothing that prepares you. Not your grandmother’s stories, not the years on the list, not the word *doctor* you hold in your mouth like a key to a door you cannot yet see.

If I had to tell you, I would say the city feels like the opposite of a block. Not because it is larger—it is—but because it hides its edges. In block seven, you know where a wall ends and where a life begins. You know the sound of footsteps that belong to someone you have already seen. The city is all edges, but they are invisible. People wear headphones, look down, live above you in boxes stacked like crates. You will think you are lonely, but you will actually be surrounded; the camp taught you the reverse.

The noise is different, too. Camps are loud with voices. Cities are loud with machines that sound like breathing. You will wait for someone to call your name and no one will, not for days. That anonymity is a strange medicine: bitter at first, then something you learn to sip carefully.

Your grandmother’s changing stories were a kind of preparation, though. They taught you that a place is not fixed. That it shifts under the tongue of the person remembering it. A city is the same. The first time, it will feel like a story she has not told yet—full of gaps you must fill in with your own imagination. You will walk down a street and invent its history because no one offers it to you. You will become the grandmother of your own new country.

And the waiting—the three years on the list, the years in block seven—has prepared your body in ways the city does not expect. Cities require a stillness that looks like movement. You already know how to make a small space feel like a universe. You know how to listen to a story that changes shape. A doctor needs this. Not just the name you say to make her happy, but the patience to hear what a patient cannot quite remember, to fill in the parts where pain has blurred the details.

So no, nothing prepares you. But you are already someone who knows how to stand at a threshold and wonder what is on the other side. That wondering is the only true preparation there is.
